RoPE rotates each adjacent coordinate pair by position times its inverse frequency. Since R(m)ᵀR(n)=R(n−m), the positional part of the query-key dot product depends on relative displacement. It does not make the content vectors themselves independent of absolute context. This convention uses adjacent pairs; some model checkpoints use a different coordinate layout. Cache decoding must use absolute token positions. Rotation preserves pair norms, which provides a useful test.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** Each pair uses $R(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}$. Since rotations compose additively, $(R(m\omega)q)^T(R(n\omega)k)=q^TR((n-m)\omega)k$. This explains the relative-position term. Verify both norm preservation and dot-product equivalence; neither alone catches every checkpoint layout mismatch. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.09864)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://towardsdatascience.com/rope-clearly-explained/) and [2](https://blog.eleuther.ai/rotary-embeddings/).
